title: Stolen Goods Sell for 70-80% of Retail. Retail Theft Is Now an Industry.
dek: Stolen merchandise passes through two layers of hands: boosters are recruited to steal from stores, fences strip the labels and resell, and the goods then go up on secondhand platforms. Networked goods fetch 70-80% of retail; T-shirts and deodorant only 30-something percent.
why: High information density: Home Depot's head of asset protection breaks down how shrink is categorised, the real P&L of locking up shelves, the pricing patterns of stolen goods, and the progress of federal legislation — plenty of hard numbers.
who: People in retail, consumer goods, supply chain and security compliance, plus investors watching US brick-and-mortar retail margins and the direction of legislation.
skip: The roughly one-minute opening plug for the LA live recording can be skipped.

points.h: A third of shrink is self-inflicted
points.body: Home Depot splits shrink into two buckets: operational/administrative and malicious — in Scott's phrasing, the things we do to ourselves and the things others do to us. At Home Depot, about 30% of shrink falls into the former, with the rest on the malicious side. The industry line that has circulated for years: of malicious shrink, roughly 40% is caused by internal employees, 35% by people who walk into the store, and the remainder is self-inflicted operational shrink. Those percentages move only a few points a year, but he thinks they are drifting upward, and that it has been under-reported ever since COVID — neither police reports nor the FBI's Uniform Crime Report capture it fully.

points.h: Employees are explicitly told not to chase anyone
points.body: The bigger problem isn't money, it's people. Scott says professional criminals often use homeless people and addicts to go into stores and steal; these people have one thing on their mind — get the goods out and turn them into cash — so they will fight, and they have fought. People have been injured in Home Depot stores, and people have been killed. So asset protection staff are trained in de-escalation, and the 400,000 store employees are explicitly told not to intervene — just back off. His attitude: he will trade shrink for human safety every single day, and management and the board back that decision.

points.h: RFID dies the moment it enters a steel store
points.body: Joe asks why RFID has been talked about for 25 years and in 2026 is still expensive and hard to scale. Scott says he doesn't understand it either, but explains Home Depot's particular problem: this is a hardware store, the store is full of steel, effectively a Faraday cage, so passive RFID can't be read — you need an active-signal solution. He also says tag cost is now essentially zero; the real bottleneck is the reading hardware — covering a 140,000-square-foot sales floor with eight separate entrances and exits costs a fortune. They have tried the idea of bricking merchandise before it leaves the store, but retrofitting an entire production line for the sake of one power drill is very hard to scale.

points.h: Stolen goods have been pushed onto secondhand platforms
points.body: The division of labour goes like this: boosters are recruited and given a list, cash, or the promise of drugs, and go steal from stores; the goods go to a fence — maybe a garage, a warehouse or a flea market — who strips the price tags, store markings and electronic tags before reselling, and the money flows up to whoever runs the operation, which might be a crew of a few people or a transnational gang. After the INFORM Act took effect in 2023, big platforms like Amazon and eBay were required to verify seller identities, so stolen goods shifted to Craigslist and Facebook Marketplace, because the law left a gap that doesn't cover peer-to-peer sellers. Home Depot works it backwards from the platforms, using models to flag sellers pricing below cost while moving large volumes.

points.h: One combo kit sold means restocking 4.2 times
points.body: Whether to lock up a shelf is a financial question. Scott says they look at the data: there's a combo kit priced at $799, and for every one sold, they have to restock 4.2 times. Take that to finance and they immediately get that it's a gross margin problem — as long as locking up breaks even or even makes a little, it's justified. But half of Home Depot's revenue comes from professional contractors, and when they break a bit on the job site, rush to the store and find it out of stock, that's a loss too. So they lock up a carefully selected set of categories, with a QR code to summon a staff member, and the average unlock takes 90 seconds; locking up doesn't necessarily hurt sales — in some categories sales actually rise, because the product is finally there.

points.h: A fake bill of lading drives the load straight out
points.body: In the supply chain he counts three plays: first, pure diversion, where a whole container is rerouted at the port or a transload warehouse and taken elsewhere, sometimes loaded back onto a container ship and sailed away; second, a driver goes eight hours across state lines, and while he sleeps someone pries open the trailer doors and unloads boxes; third, forged bills of lading and pickup orders, made to look real with AI, where a driver pulls in, says he's picking up a certain trailer, and just drives off. He says what's new isn't necessarily the method, it's the volume, because these cases are very hard to pursue. Rail is the piece that has clearly worsened over the past five or six years — cars sitting in a yard get pried open by a group; and their intelligence is good, they don't touch every car, only the one carrying guns or electronics.

points.h: In security, AI is an efficiency tool
points.body: Scott says they have more cases than they can investigate, so for them AI is an efficiency question: a typical organized retail crime case takes an average of 70 days from discovery to closure and handover to police, and compressing that cycle means they can work more cases. They have just replaced the video management system across all 2,300 stores, letting existing cameras run edge analytics — identifying people who linger too long in an area, deliberately avoid staff, or show up where they shouldn't be. He also admits that to identify a particular combination of suspicious behaviours and then identify the specific person, he doesn't have enough cameras yet, but they will get there. Separately, they have an in-house company doing web scraping.

points.h: Seven years ago nobody cared; now there's a federal bill
points.body: He says he is very optimistic now. INFORM is arguably the first federal bill driven by organized retail crime, and next is CORCA (Combating Organized Retail Crime Act): the retail industry broadly supports it, it has bipartisan co-sponsorship, it has passed the House, it's attached to the NDAA awaiting Senate passage, and the president has said he will sign it. The rationale is that this crime is inherently interstate — it happens in Cobb County, Georgia, and the goods flow to South Carolina and North Carolina, which is interstate transportation of stolen property, but there were no corresponding federal resources; the bill would provide resources, prosecutors and a coordination centre. Seven years ago he was thoroughly pessimistic about this: nobody took it seriously, and the prevailing mood was decriminalisation and defunding the police.

terms.def: Inventory is on the books but doesn't match up at count; includes both operational error and theft.
Group theft across stores and even states, for the purpose of reselling for profit.
Recruited shoplifters who are given a list, cash or the promise of drugs and go into stores specifically to steal.
The middleman who consolidates stolen goods, strips the markings and price tags, and resells them.
Took effect in 2023; requires online platforms to verify the identity of high-volume sellers, with peer-to-peer sellers excluded.
Having the cameras themselves analyse footage in real time, to spot behaviours like lingering or avoiding staff.
